newsitem.title: USA: U.S. doubles food aid to N. Korea, visit planned.
newsitem.headline: U.S. doubles food aid to N. Korea, visit planned.

text.p: With peace talks less than one month away, the United States on Monday doubled its food aid to North Korea and said two respected former senior U.S. officials would soon make a private visit to Pyongyang.

Following the latest urgent appeal by the U.N. World Food Programme, Washington pledged $27 million in food aid, bringing to $52 million its contribution for the year. Since 1995, the United States has donated a total of $60.4 million.

The aid is intended to combat widespread malnutrition, particularly among children, caused by several years of severe flooding that have compounded the problems of North Korea's hardline communist system.

"In response to the World Food Program's announcement of July 9 of an expanded appeal for humanitarian food aid for children in North Korea, the United States government has decided to extend 100,000 metric tonnes of grain valued at approximately $27 million," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
The latest offer is for more than half of the $46 million requested in the latest WFP appeal.
Of the latest U.S. donation, 45,000 metric tonnes of grain will be monitored by the WFP and used to feed children age 6 and under in nurseries, kindergartens and orphanages.
The other 55,000 tons will be monitored by up to 15 U.S. private voluntary organisations who will work in conjunction with WFP to help the elderly, as well as children, Burns said.
The executive director of the WFP said in Rome last week that donors had met almost one-third of the latest appeal.

Washington denies its emergency food aid is linked with peace talks for the divided Korean peninsula. But officials hope their quick and increasingly generous responses to North Korea's needs persuade Pyongyang that Washington takes its food crisis seriously, is sincere in trying to help out and there is a benefit to working with the United States.
Officials also hope this will enhance the climate for the peace talks.

The United States, North Korea, its arch-rival South Korea and China are to meet in New York on Aug. 5 to decide details on negotiations aimed at closing the books on the 1950-53 Korean War by replacing a fraying armistice with a formal peace treaty.

Burns also said on Monday that former Sen. Sam Nunn, who once headed the Senate Armed Services Committee and is a respected American voice on national security issues, and James Laney, who just retired as U.S. ambassador to South Korea, had been invited to visit North Korea on July 20-22.
Nunn and Laney have been briefed by the U.S. State Department and will be accompanied by two experts from the State and the Defence Department.

"It is a private visit -- but it's important -- because both (men) ... are senior respected figures who can convey a straight message from the United States to North Korea in advance of the four-party preparatory meeting on August 5. So we do very much support their trip," Burns said.

He said Nunn and Laney would explain "the fundamentals of U.S. policy, including the historic opportunity we have now to engage with the North and South with China to make sure that these four-party talks will actually go forward, and will lead to ... a cessation of the Korean conflict, a formal cessation, a peace treaty after so many years."
Also, Burns said the two former officials would discuss food aid, the 1994 U.S.-North Korea nuclear agreement, and "other issues in U.S.-North Korean relations."

U.S. officials said Nunn and Laney will not negotiate on any issue while in Pyongyang. The administration encourages such contacts as a means of expanding U.S. ties with one of the world's most opaque societies and providing alternate ways of getting the U.S. message across.
